nameStory: The Scissor-tailed Flycatcher gets its name from its spectacular deeply forked tail that opens and closes like a pair of scissors during flight. When the bird spreads its long, streaming tail feathers wide, it creates an unmistakable silhouette that looks remarkably like an open pair of scissors cutting through the sky.
description: The Scissor-tailed Flycatcher is a striking medium-sized songbird with one of the most dramatic tails in North America. This elegant flycatcher has a pale gray head and back, white underparts with salmon-pink sides and wing linings, and most memorably, an extremely long, deeply forked black and white tail that can be nearly as long as the rest of its body. Like other flycatchers, it catches insects on the wing, often returning to the same perch repeatedly.

idTips.label: Deeply forked tail
idTips.description: The tail is spectacularly long and forked, appearing black with white outer edges that flash prominently in flight - no other New England bird has such dramatic tail streamers

idTips.label: Salmon-pink wash
idTips.description: Look for peachy-pink or salmon coloring on the sides of the belly and especially bright pink wing linings visible when the bird flies

idTips.label: Pale gray and white body
idTips.description: The head and back are soft pearl-gray while the throat and belly are clean white, creating a crisp, elegant appearance

idTips.label: Flycatcher behavior
idTips.description: Sits upright on prominent perches like fence posts or power lines, then darts out to catch flying insects with an audible snap of the bill

idTips.label: Acrobatic flight
idTips.description: Performs spectacular aerial displays with the long tail opening and closing like scissors, sometimes tumbling or rolling through the air

habitat: In New England, Scissor-tailed Flycatchers are extremely rare visitors, occasionally appearing in open areas like fields, pastures, and agricultural lands during migration. They prefer areas with scattered trees or utility lines for perching, avoiding dense forests in favor of the kind of open country with fence posts and power lines that characterizes their Great Plains breeding grounds.

seasonality.spring: Very rarely seen during spring migration in May, when lost individuals might overshoot their normal Great Plains destinations and end up in New England's open country.
seasonality.summer: Exceptional summer records exist, with individual birds sometimes staying for weeks in suitable open habitat, delighting birders with their spectacular aerial displays.
seasonality.fall: Fall sightings are slightly more likely than spring, typically in September when young birds dispersing from breeding areas might wander far from their normal range.
seasonality.winter: Not found in New England during winter, as these birds migrate to Central America and are not equipped for cold New England temperatures.

funFact: Oklahoma chose the Scissor-tailed Flycatcher as its state bird partly because the males perform jaw-dropping courtship flights, climbing up to 100 feet in the air before tumbling earthward in a series of zigzag dives and barrel rolls, all while showing off their spectacular scissor tails - it's like watching a feathered aerial acrobat!
confusionNotes: The incredibly long, forked tail makes this species unmistakable - no other bird in New England comes close to having such dramatic tail streamers. The only potential confusion might be with a Fork-tailed Flycatcher, an even rarer vagrant, but that species lacks the salmon-pink coloring and has an all-black tail.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a flycatcher, this species belongs to the Tyrant Flycatcher family, which is completely different from the Old World flycatchers - it's a case of similar feeding behavior leading to the same common name for unrelated bird families.
compareHints: Among its kingbird relatives, the Scissor-tailed Flycatcher is instantly distinguished by its extraordinarily long, forked tail - Eastern Kingbirds have much shorter, square tails with white tips, while Western Kingbirds have moderately long tails but nothing approaching the dramatic streamers of the Scissor-tailed. The salmon-pink wash on the sides is also unique among the kingbirds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern Kingbirds are the only kingbird species that regularly breeds in New England, making identification easier than in western regions where multiple kingbird species overlap.
Western Kingbirds are easily distinguished from their Eastern Kingbird cousins by their bright yellow underparts versus the Eastern's clean white belly.
Among the kingbirds, Tropical Kingbird's bright yellow belly immediately separates it from the white-bellied Eastern Kingbird.
Unlike its kingbird relatives, the Fork-tailed Flycatcher has that unmistakable extremely long, forked tail that no other kingbird possesses.
Unlike Eastern Kingbirds with their stark black caps and white tail bands, Gray Kingbirds are much more subtly colored in pale gray and white.
Unlike the familiar Eastern Kingbird with its clean white underparts and white-tipped tail, Cassin's Kingbird shows the distinctive white throat against gray chest pattern.
